Title: Microbenchmarks - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
Microbenchmarks are custom tests designed to evaluate specific components of a GPU, such as the instruction pipeline or global memory, by measuring their performance metrics like throughput. Microbenchmarks are designed to serve as specific stressors that sensitize targeted processor chips to particular failure modes under harsh environments, enabling the identification or diagnosis of deficiencies in traditional architecture performance metrics such as instructions per cycle and cache misses, as well as power or energy-related metrics, temperature and lifetime reliability, and resilience under transient errors. In the context of graphics processing unit (GPU) kernel performance, custom microbenchmarks are constructed to exercise different components of the target GPU, such as the instruction pipeline or global memory, and measure their throughput. Microbenchmarks are also applied to evaluate central processing unit (CPU) instruction throughput, memory latency and bandwidth, and cache behavior, as well as to construct power models for individual sub-units by correlating performance monitoring counters with empirical power measurements. Within Internet of Things (IoT) deployments, microbenchmarks provide useful information for understanding the performance of subsystems associated with smart objects, identifying architectural bottlenecks, and enabling hardware and software engineers to compare and assess design trade-offs at the component level. In GPU performance modeling, custom microbenchmarks are used to measure throughput and exercise different components such as instruction pipelines and global memory. In large-scale Internet of Things deployments, microbenchmarks provide useful information to understand subsystem performance, identify architectural bottlenecks, and allow engineers to compare and assess design trade-offs at the component level. The design of microbenchmarks requires flexibility and generality, allowing users to control code generation at the assembly level and specify both high-level and dynamic properties, such as loads per instruction and instructions per cycle ratio. The “architecture back-end” consists of three components: (a) definition of the instruction set architecture via op code syntax table, as well as the high-level parametric definition of the processor microarchitecture; (b) an analytical reference model that is able to calculate (precisely or within specified bounds) the performance and unit-level utilization levels of a candidate loop microbenchmark; (c) a (micro)architecture translator segment that is responsible for final (micro)architecture-specific consolidation and integration of the microbenchmark program.

Stack Overflow for Teams is now called **Stack Internal**. ##### Collectives™ on Stack Overflow. # How to calculate the achieved bandwidth of a CUDA kernel. I want a measure of how much of the peak memory bandwidth my kernel archives. Say I have a NVIDIA Tesla C1060, which has a max Bandwidth of 102.4 GB/s. In my kernel I have the following accesses to global memory:. float result = (in_data[index]-loc_mem[k]) * (in_data[index]-loc_mem[k]);. I count for each thread 4000\*2+2 accesses to global memory. Having 1.000.000 threads and all accesses are float I have ~32GB of global memory accesses (inbound and outbound added). As my kernel only takes 0.1s I would archive ~320GB/s which is higher than the max bandwidth, thus there is an error in my calculations / assumptions. I assume, CUDA does some caching, so not all memory accesses count. - When 4194304Bytes = 4Bytes \* 1024\*1024 data points = 4MB and `gpu_time` ~= 0.1 s then I achieve a bandwidth of 10\*40MB/s = 400MB/s. p.s. Tell me if you need other counters for your answer. sister question: How to calculate Gflops of a kernel. ## 1 Answer 1. Default counters in Visual Profiler gives you enough information to get an idea about your kernel (memory bandwidth, shared memory bank conflicts, instructions executed...). Regarding to your question, to calculate the achieved global memory throughput:. Global memory read throughput in giga-bytes per second. For **compute capability < 2.0** this is calculated as (((gld\_32\*32) + (gld\_64\*64) + (gld\_128\*128)) \* TPC) / gputime For **compute capability >= 2.0** this is calculated as ((DRAM reads) \* 32) / gputime. ## Your Answer. Title: Memory Bandwidth - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
Profiling tools like perf\_event can be employed to measure the time required for the processor to read and write contiguous blocks of data, enabling calculation of the processor’s memory bandwidth and providing values for performance upper bounds. The roofline model is throughput-oriented and independent of instruction set architecture, dividing performance into regions bounded by peak performance and memory bandwidth; computations below the memory bandwidth bound are limited by data movement, while those below the peak performance bound are constrained by computational capacity. Memory bandwidth is a key gating factor for application performance, where the rate at which data can be moved between memory and processing units directly affects throughput and efficiency. Hardware-software collaborative optimizations in modern GPU architectures include kernel optimization, operator fusion, and key-value caching, which maximize parallel processing and memory bandwidth utilization. Frameworks like Core-Assisted Bottleneck Acceleration (CABA) utilize idle on-chip resources to alleviate memory bandwidth bottlenecks by employing assist warps for tasks such as data compression, resulting in an average performance improvement of 41.7% across memory-bandwidth-sensitive GPU applications. In contrast, general-purpose processors must satisfy requirements from legacy operating systems, applications, and I/O devices that present more challenges to supporting parallel memory accesses and thus make it more difficult to increase the throughput of memory accesses, commonly referred to as memory bandwidth . CABA enables the use of idle computational units and pipelines to alleviate the memory bandwidth bottleneck, for example, by using assist warps to perform data compression to transfer less data from memory. Our extensive evaluations show that CABA, when used to implement data compression, provides on average a performance improvement of 41.7% (as high as 2.6×) across a variety of memory-bandwidth-sensitive general-purpose GPU applications. Key-Value Cache reduces repeated computations in transformer models by storing previously computed vectors, Kernel Optimization enhances memory bandwidth utilization through various techniques, and Operator Fusion reduces memory access times by merging operations. Suppose you have a memory bound GPU kernel, how close can you get to the stated theoretical bandwidth of the GPU? Even in Mark Harris's Optimising Parallel Reduction presentation he 'only' gets 63GB/sec which is about 73% of the bandwidth of his test GPU (a G80) which he claimed 84.6GB/sec peak bandwidth. "throughput is memory-bandwidth limited, sustaining around 75% of the. 144 GB/s peak memory bandwidth, compared to a practical limit of 85%. If so, what other factors (supposing you have a very well optimised kernel) would prevent you from reaching theoretical peak bandwidth? A similar thread: GPU Memory bandwidth theoretical vs practical. on GeForce GT 710 I got 0.9 of the theoretical bandwidth. Thanks for contributing an answer to Stack Overflow!
